participation.text: Mass organizing and elections brought the CPP into office before independence; regional opponents contested the distribution of power.

evidence.text: An overprinted stamp shows a public design; a policy statement records intended priorities. Neither establishes how every household experienced independence.

change.text: Independence in 1957 retained a monarchy; the republic followed in 1960, and later repression requires a separate assessment of political freedom.

production.text: Market women helped carry political messages, while cocoa production figured in national development arguments.

name: Ghana: from organizing for independence to governing
place: Gold Coast and independent Ghana; Accra
geographicPrecision: Accra is a political and archival anchor, not a map of every movement or the boundaries of colonial jurisdictions.

interval.label: Political mobilization, 1948–1957; republic in 1960
interval.note: Selected route to independence and early constitutional choices. Earlier resistance and later Ghanaian history extend beyond this inquiry.

question: How did people turn a demand for self-government into a government?
summary: On a 1957 stamp, “Ghana Independence” is printed across an older Gold Coast design. The new words announce a political change; the cocoa workers and royal portrait underneath invite questions about what continued. Independence on 6 March 1957 followed years of organizing, elections and argument over who should govern, how power should be shared and what freedom should accomplish.

sections.title: Grievances became organized politics
sections.text: After the Second World War, shortages, inflation and difficult employment conditions sharpened discontent in the Gold Coast. Farmers, veterans and urban residents had different grievances. The United Gold Coast Convention, founded in 1947, demanded self-government and recruited Nkrumah as its general secretary. Unrest in 1948 prompted detention of leaders and a new constitutional inquiry. This sequence connects everyday pressures with institutional change without making every protest the work of one party or one leader.

citations.locator: Return to the Gold Coast and UGCC

sections.title: A party needed people and communication
sections.text: Nkrumah broke with the UGCC and formed the Convention People’s Party in 1949. Its call for immediate self-government appealed to workers, farmers, young people and others dissatisfied with gradual change. Market women were important supporters and channels of communication through local trading networks. The party’s strength therefore depended on repeated work—organizing meetings, spreading messages and sustaining support—as well as public speeches. The 1950 Positive Action campaign called for strikes and nonviolent resistance; disturbances and arrests followed, and Nkrumah was imprisoned.

sections.title: Winning office was not yet independence
sections.text: The CPP won the 1951 election while Nkrumah was still in prison. He was released and invited to lead government business. Constitutional changes in 1952 and 1954 increased elected ministers’ responsibility, but defense and foreign affairs remained with the colonial governor. This distinction matters: African ministers could administer much of the country while Britain retained important powers. Elections, participation in government and national independence were connected steps, not interchangeable labels.

sections.title: Independence did not mean one opinion
sections.text: The CPP favored a centralized state. The Asante-based National Liberation Movement advocated a federation with more regional power and worked with the Northern People’s Party. After the contested 1956 election, a legislative motion sought independence. On 6 March 1957 the Gold Coast became independent Ghana; Nkrumah remained prime minister. Elizabeth II was initially head of state, represented by a governor-general. The 1960 constitution made Ghana a republic. The royal portrait on the independence stamp is therefore evidence worth investigating, not simply a printing mistake.

sections.title: What should political freedom provide?
sections.text: In his parliamentary statement on the eve of independence, Nkrumah linked national policy to economic and social development and to the freedom of other African peoples. He pointed to cocoa farming and resources for development, including Tema Harbour. These were political claims and priorities presented by a prime minister, not an independent audit of prosperity. The stamp’s cocoa scene helps pose the next questions: who produced export income, who decided how to spend it, and which communities gained services or influence?

sections.title: Follow the promise into the institutions
sections.text: Early independence also brought restrictions on opposition. The 1958 Preventive Detention Act permitted detention without trial, and Ghana formally became a one-party state in 1964. These developments complicate an account that stops at celebration. National sovereignty and freedom to challenge a government are different historical questions. Investigating both preserves the achievement of ending colonial rule while asking how power was exercised afterward.

deeperReading.title: A stamp is a small public surface
deeperReading.text: The overprint places a new national name and a date on an existing postal design. Under it remain the words Gold Coast, Elizabeth II’s profile and a scene labelled Breaking Cocoa Pods. You can observe those elements directly. Interpreting them requires a second step: the independence constitution retained the monarchy, while cocoa connected people’s agricultural work to public revenue and plans for development. The stamp is useful evidence of what officials circulated, but its tidy composition does not show wages, land tenure or how actual workers felt about independence.

deeperReading.title: A primary voice and a later account
deeperReading.text: Nkrumah spoke to the Legislative Assembly late on 5 March 1957, with independence expected at midnight. His government policy statement explains the powers he intended to assume and the place he wanted Ghana to occupy internationally. A later country study can follow subsequent legislation and conflict, but it has its own authorship, date and judgments. Read the two for different purposes: one shows a leader making an argument at a decisive moment; the other organizes later evidence into an explanation. Neither cancels the need for opponents’ accounts and local histories.

deeperReading.title: Where this account needs widening
deeperReading.text: The country study describes regional opposition and disagreement over the incorporation of British Togoland, but a detailed border history needs the plebiscite records and situated Ewe accounts. They are not supplied here. Likewise, market women appear as political organizers in the synthesis without individual voices in the sources displayed. Those are specific next research tasks. Ghana’s inclusion strengthens one modern African inquiry; it cannot stand in for the many different routes to independence elsewhere on the continent.

claims.text: Ghana became independent on 6 March 1957 and a republic in 1960; independence did not initially end the monarchy.

familyActivity.explanation: An object can carry several layers of history. Observation supplies questions; a dated constitutional account helps answer them.

evidenceReading.title: Read the eve-of-independence debate
evidenceReading.introduction: These editorial paraphrases come from the scanned Legislative Assembly debate of 5 March 1957, not the separate outdoor independence speech. The page and column numbers allow a precise return to the source.

items.label: Which powers changed hands? — paraphrase
items.text: Nkrumah describes internal self-government while defense and foreign affairs still belonged to the governor; he says he will take those portfolios at independence.
items.interpretation: The speaker identifies a concrete institutional change. Holding elected office before 1957 was not the same as controlling all state powers.

items.label: What should independence do? — paraphrase
items.text: He argues for development of national resources and support for African peoples seeking freedom and social progress.
items.interpretation: This tells us what the prime minister publicly advocated. Whether policies achieved those aims needs evidence from later budgets, services, political institutions and people’s lives.

review.reviewer: Codex source consultation and self-review; not independent historian approval
review.scope: Bounded local teaching account; cited source passages and image records consulted.
limitations: The parliamentary scan was visually consulted at the cited pages; no complete transcription or exhaustive debate review is claimed.
Named market organizers, opposition voices, local economic evidence and the British Togoland/Ewe history need further research.
The Library of Congress study dates to 1995; its evaluative language is not adopted wholesale. No claim that Ghana was the first independent African state is made.

returnPrompt: Name one power that changed in 1957 and one kind of freedom that still needs its own evidence.

placeStudy.title: Ghana: a capital, a regional challenge and a development project
placeStudy.description: Three places connect political institutions, debate over regional authority and plans for economic development. Close coastal locations group on a small screen; each remains available by name. No colonial or modern borders are reconstructed.

points.label: Accra — assembly and political organizing
points.text: Accra was a center of political activity and the legislative debate. The 5 March 1957 statement identifies the governmental powers due to change at independence.

points.label: Kumasi / Asante — regional opposition
points.text: The Asante-based National Liberation Movement argued for a federation with stronger regional powers. Kumasi is an orientation point for the Asante region, not a claim that everyone there held one opinion.

points.label: Tema — plans for a harbour
points.text: Nkrumah cited the building of Tema Harbour in his independence-eve account of development financing. This is a project named in the 1957 speech, not a claim that the completed harbour opened that year.
